newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romania votes in presidential run-off contest.
newsitem.headline: Romania votes in presidential run-off contest.

text.p: Romania votes on Sunday in a presidential run-off contest, after opposition centrists beat ex-communists in parliamentary polls earlier this month.
After seven years in office, President Ion Iliescu faces a tough battle against academic Emil Constantinescu. Iliescu was only four points ahead of Constantinescu in the first round.
The following are key facts about Romania:
POPULATION: 22.66 million. This includes 1.6 million Hungarians (7.1 percent), 400,000 Gypsies (1.8 percent), 119,000 Germans (0.5 percent).

RELIGION: Most Romanians (some 86.8 percent) belong to the country's Orthodox Church. Five percent of the population are Roman Catholics, 3.5 percent Reformed Church, and one percent Greek-Catholics. There are 9,000 Jews under a chief rabbi.
LANGUAGE: The official language is Romanian.

AREA: 237,500 sq km (91,699 sq miles). Romania is bounded north and northeast by Ukraine and Moldova, east by the Black Sea, south by Bulgaria, southwest by former Yugoslavia and northwest by Hungary.
CAPITAL: Bucharest (population 2.06 million).

ARMED FORCES: Romania was a member of the Soviet-led Warsaw Pact military alliance. It has joined NATO's Partnership for Peace programme and applied for membership of the alliance. Total armed forces: Active: 217,400 (104,700 conscripts).

ECONOMY: Per capita GDP was $1,570 in 1995, down from $2,446 in 1980. Romania, potentially one of Europe's richest farm areas with ample crude oil supplies, was reduced to one of the region's poorest states by a bungled self-sufficiency policy under communism. President Nicolae Ceausescu cleared Romania's $11 billion foreign debt in the 1980s, throttling imports of industrial equipment and diverting food to export.
After his fall in December 1989, there was an abrupt decline until October 1992 when trade began to recover.

Private enterprise now makes up 45 percent of GDP and external trade and over half of retail business. But under Prime Minister Nicolae Vacaroiu, appointed in 1992, little real progress was made in privatising industry.

Foreign investors have put only $2 billion into Romania in seven years. After inflation of 300 percent in 1993, Romania cut the figure back to 27.8 percent in 1995. But pre-election largesse has pushed inflation to 45.3 percent. Unemployment, unknown under communists, is still low at 5.9 percent.
The International Monetary Fund initially enjoyed good relations with Romania but suspended credits this year.
HISTORY: Romania was a loose alliance of principalities, prey to the territorial rivalry of Austro-Hungary, Russia and Turkey until it became a kingdom in 1881.

It fought the Germans in World War One and in the inter-war years constitutional monarchy prevailed. In World War Two, Romania fought with the Axis, then changed sides in 1944 and fell under Moscow's sway. Communists forced the king to abdicate in 1947 and banished him abroad.
Romania was under communist dictatorship from 1947 to 1989 when Ceausescu was deposed by party dissidents and army officers and shot in a bloody popular uprising.
Iliescu took power, the communist state was abolised and elections held in May 1990. Several outbursts of political violence have since rocked Romania. Critics blame Iliescu.
In December 1991 Romania formally became a French-style presidential republic. Iliescu was re-elected in 1992 and his Party of Social Democracy won a majority.
The PDSR was defeated by the centre opposition Democratic Convention bloc in parliamentary elections in early November.
